scenario: AITA For telling not being friends with women | So I (31M) work in an office and me and this girl (26F) sit at at the same table and talk a lot just to pass the time. Recently she has started asking me to go out for drinks on Friday after work (as friends not a date). I made excuses why I could not for a couple of weeks, but then she asked me if I disliked her, I thought I would just tell her the truth that I do not do friendships with women. I do not recall what I said verbatim however the gist of it is that, if I spend prolonged time with a woman I start feeling for a lack of a better word 'territorial'. If they start talking with other guys or get attention from them I my intestines start roiling and I feel an extreme sense of agitation (I never act on it and I put on a happy face and persevere) however I hate said feeling and prefer to avoid it and hence I do not do friendships with women. She then said I should see a psychologist (I will not, even though I am flawed, my flaws make up a part of who I am and I do not wish to change), and since then for the past couple of weeks our talking has just been work related. I thought it would be best to be honest however I am thinking maybe I should have made up some excuse. AITA? Addendum I do get same feelings at work however I do not think about work at home and its work so I have no choice but to tolerate them. However I do not wish to put myself through unnecessary discomfort willingly outside of work. I do not wish to feel this way, I know it is not correct, again I never act on it, but I can not help feeling it. I had told this story to a guy I know and he said I must have been be controlling with my previous girlfriends. So just in case people here will make that assumption, it could not be further from the truth. If the lady is already mine I do not mind her talking to or being around other guys, I think because I know she is mine it makes me happy thinking other men might want what I have and can not have it.

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently and create a warm, festive atmosphere: ### **1. Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! Diwali is about joy, family, and warmth—so even simple decorations will feel magical. **Shubh Diwali!** 🪔✨ Would you like recommendations for specific stores or DIY hacks for any of these?

Honesty vs. Cruelty** - **Honesty is important**, but **brutal honesty without empathy is cruel**. You didn’t just say, *"I don’t do friendships with women"*—you explained it in a way that framed her as the problem (your "territorial" feelings are her fault for existing). This is **emotionally dismissive** and **invalidates her feelings**. - **Example**: Telling someone they’re "too much work" or "triggering" for you to be friends isn’t a neutral observation—it’s a **personal preference dressed as a fact**, which can feel like a rejection. - **Comparison**: If a woman said to a man, *"I don’t do friendships with men because I get jealous when you talk to other women,"* it would sound **absurdly possessive and unfair**. Your situation is the same, just reversed. - **Your feelings are valid**, but **they don’t justify shutting down a friendship**. If you can tolerate this at work (as you said), why not outside of it? **Work is a different context**—it’s temporary, structured, and not a personal relationship. Outside of work, you’re choosing to **avoid discomfort** by cutting off a potential friendship, which is a **cop-out**. --- ### **2. The "Territorial" Feeling: What Does It Really Mean?** You describe this as a **physical/emotional reaction** to women interacting with other men. This is **not just jealousy**—it’s a **deep-seated insecurity** that likely stems from: - **Fear of abandonment** (e.g., *"If she talks to others, she might leave me"*). - **Lack of trust** in your own worth (e.g., *"I need to prove I’m the only one she wants"*). - **Social conditioning** (e.g., being raised to believe men should be "exclusive" in relationships, even in friendships). **This is not a personality flaw—it’s a pattern of behavior that needs addressing.** - You say you **never act on it**, but **suppressing feelings doesn’t make them disappear**. They’ll resurface in other relationships. - Your addendum about being fine with women you’re "already mine" talking to other guys is **hypocritical**. If you truly believed in equality, you’d **not demand exclusivity in friendships** just because you’re in a relationship. **Key Question**: *Would you feel the same way if a man said to you, "I don’t do friendships with women because I get territorial when they talk to other men"?* - If the answer is **no**, then your behavior is **sexist and unfair**. --- ### **3. The Impact on Her** - **She felt rejected**. You didn’t just end the friendship—you **explained why she was unworthy** of it. That’s **emotionally damaging**, especially if she was genuinely interested in being friends. - **You dismissed her suggestion to see a psychologist**. This is **defensive and avoidant**. If you’re struggling with these feelings, **own it** instead of shoving it under the rug. - **Workplace dynamics**: Even if you’re not dating her, **how you treat her outside work affects how she treats you at work**. If she feels used or disrespected, her behavior toward you may change (e.g., less engagement, more professionalism). --- ### **4. The "I Don’t Change" Argument** You said: > *"I am flawed, my flaws make up a part of who I am and I do not wish to change."* This is **self-defeating**. **Flaws are not immutable**—they’re **patterns we can unlearn**. Here’s why: - **You tolerate this at work**—so why not outside? **Work is a different context**, but **your behavior is still unfair**. - **You say you never act on it**, but **suppressing feelings doesn’t make them go away**. They’ll **escalate** in future relationships. - **True confidence** comes from **not needing to control others**. If you’re truly secure, you’d **not care if she talked to other men**—because you’d trust her and yourself. **Alternative Approach**: Instead of saying *"I don’t do friendships with women,"* try: - *"I’m not great at friendships right now because I’m dealing with some personal stuff. I’d love to stay friends, but I need to focus on myself for a while."* - *"I’m not the best person to be friends with right now because I get overwhelmed easily. I hope we can still be professional at work."* This **acknowledges the issue without blaming her**. --- ### **5. The "I’m Not Controlling" Claim** You said: > *"If the lady is already mine I do not mind her talking to or being around other guys... If I know she is mine it makes me happy thinking other men might want what I have and can not have it."* This is **a double standard**: - **In a relationship**, you’re **fine with her talking to other men** because you **own her**. - **In a friendship**, you **demand exclusivity** because you **don’t own her**. This is **not about control—it’s about insecurity**. **True security** means **not needing to "own" anyone**, whether in friendship or romance. --- ### **6. Psychological Perspective** Your feelings sound like **attachment anxiety** (fear of abandonment) or **insecure attachment style**. Here’s how to reframe it: - **Jealousy in friendships** is often a **red flag for deeper issues**. If you can’t trust a friend to have other relationships, **you’re not ready for a healthy friendship**. - **Territorial feelings** are **not natural**—they’re **learned behaviors**. If you grew up in a household where men were possessive, you may have internalized that as "normal." - **Solution**: **Therapy** (even if you don’t want to admit it). A psychologist can help you **understand where these feelings come from** and **learn to manage them**. --- ### **7. Ethical Considerations** From an **ethical standpoint**, this behavior is **unfair** because: - **You’re imposing your insecurities on her**. She didn’t ask to be your emotional punching bag. - **You’re avoiding accountability**. Instead of saying *"I have issues I need to work on,"* you **blame her for existing**. - **You’re setting a bad precedent**. If you treat women this way in friendships, **how will you treat them in relationships?** --- ### **What You Could Have Done Instead** 1. **Be honest but kind**: - *"I’ve been dealing with some personal stuff lately and I’m not great at friendships right now. I’d love to stay professional at work, but I need to focus on myself for a while."* - This **acknowledges the issue without making her the problem**. 2. **Redirect the conversation**: - If she asked to hang out, say: *"I’d love to, but I’m not really in the mood for socializing right now. Maybe another time?"* - This **avoids a full explanation** and **doesn’t burn bridges**. 3. **Work on yourself**: - **Journal** about why you feel this way. - **Watch her interact with others**—do you really have a reason to be jealous, or is it just insecurity? - **Practice trust exercises** (e.g., imagine her talking to other men—does it really bother you, or are you just afraid of losing her?). --- ### **Final Verdict: 0/1** **0 (Not Acceptable)**. This isn’t just "AITA"—it’s **selfish, unfair, and emotionally immature**. You’re **avoiding responsibility** by: - **Blaming her** for your feelings. - **Refusing to address the root cause** (your insecurities). - **Cutting off a potential friendship** because you’re **too afraid to face your discomfort**. **True growth comes from:** ✅ **Acknowledging your flaws** (instead of denying them). ✅ **Not shifting blame** (you’re the one with the issue, not her). ✅ **Working on yourself** (so you don’t repeat this in future relationships). --- ### **How to Move Forward** 1. **Apologize (if you feel guilty)**: - *"I realize I handled that poorly. I shouldn’t have made it about my feelings—it was unfair to you."* - (Even if she doesn’t accept it, **owning your mistake is mature**.) 2. **Reflect on why this happened**: - Why did you feel the need to **explain your feelings in such a way**? - What **fear** were you trying to avoid? 3. **Challenge your beliefs**: - *"Do I really need to control who she talks to?"* - *"Is this about her, or is this about my own insecurities?"* 4. **Consider therapy**: - If you’re **not willing to change**, at least **understand why** you feel this way. Therapy can help you **unlearn these patterns**. 5. **Practice trust**: - Next time you see her talking to other men, **observe without reacting**. Ask yourself: - *"Does this really bother me, or am I just afraid of losing her?"* - *"Would I feel the same way if she were a man?"* --- ### **Key Takeaway** You’re **not a bad person**, but **this behavior is unhealthy**. **True confidence** doesn’t come from **controlling others**—it comes from **trusting yourself**. If you can’t **tolerate a woman talking to other men in friendship**, then **you’re not ready for healthy relationships**—romantic or otherwise. Would you feel the same way if a **man** said to you, *"I don’t do friendships with men because I get territorial when they talk to other women"*? If not, **why is it okay for you but not for her?** **You have the power to change. Start by being honest with yourself—not just with others.**
